title: Avoiding Explicit Matrix Inversion
markdown:
## What this covers

Problem Set 7 in Stat 243 (Statistical Computing, UC Berkeley) is built around one question: given
a linear-algebra computation that could be written down using an inverse, how do you actually
compute it, and how much does the honest way cost compared with the naive way? The problems attach
to the course's Unit 10 on numerical linear algebra — Gaussian elimination and the $LU$
decomposition, the Cholesky decomposition, condition numbers, and sparse-matrix storage — which
this problem set assumes but does not re-derive, and which is not itself supplied here. This
chapter reads the Fall 2024 and Fall 2025 versions of PS7 together: the specific problems differ
from year to year, but every one of them is an instance of the same principle, applied to a
different statistical estimator.

Assumes: matrix multiplication and Gaussian-elimination/back-substitution costs stated in terms of
$n$, what a symmetric positive-definite matrix and a Cholesky factor are, and what an eigenvalue is.

## The principle behind every problem: factor once, solve, don't invert

Both years open by asking students to count operations rather than just code something up. Fall
2024's Problem 1 states the fact Unit 10 already established: solving $Ax=b$ by Gaussian
elimination (the $LU$ decomposition) costs $n^3/3$ operations, ignoring lower-order terms. The
problem then asks for the cost of the "obvious" alternative — computing $A^{-1}$ explicitly by
solving $AZ=I$ (the way `numpy.linalg.inv` actually works, via the LAPACK routine `dgesv`), and
then forming $x=Zb$ by matrix-vector multiplication — broken into three pieces: the elimination
step turning $AZ=I$ into $UZ=I^*$, the backsolve for $Z$, and the final multiplication $Zb$. Adding
these counts up and comparing the total to $n^3/3$ turns "you shouldn't invert matrices" from a
slogan into a quantitative statement.

Fall 2025 asks the symmetric-positive-definite version of the same question. Problem 1 asks for the
exact operation count of the Cholesky decomposition — the constant in front of $n^3$, not just the
order — to compare against the count given in the notes. Problem 2 then times three ways of solving
$x=A^{-1}b$ for a positive-definite $A$ — `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`, `np.linalg.solve(A, b)`, and a
Cholesky factorization followed by two triangular solves — at $n=5000$, and asks whether the
ordering of the timings matches the ordering of the operation counts. The problem hands over one
piece of the comparison directly: inverting a general matrix via the $LU$ decomposition costs
$4n^3/3$, well above the $n^3/3$ needed to solve the system once.

The two years test the same fact from two corners of Unit 10 — general $LU$ versus
symmetric-positive-definite Cholesky — and the exercise in both cases is the same kind of
bookkeeping: add up the elimination cost, the solve cost, and any extra multiplication, and compare
the total against the cost of solving the system directly.

## Not inverting on purpose: GLS, 2SLS, and constrained least squares

The rest of each problem set applies that principle to a statistical estimator whose formula on
paper contains one or more matrix inverses that a working implementation should never form
explicitly.

**Generalized least squares** (Fall 2024, Problem 2). The GLS estimator
$$\hat{\beta}=(X^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}Y$$
has $X$ of size $n\times p$ and $\Sigma$ an $n\times n$ positive-definite matrix, with $n$ in the
thousands and $p$ in the hundreds. Read literally, the formula asks for two inverses, of an
$n\times n$ and a $p\times p$ matrix. The problem asks for pseudo-code and then a `gls()` function
that computes $\hat\beta$ using factorizations and solves rather than either inverse, followed by a
timed comparison against the version that actually calls the inverse (computed only once, and
multiplied in an efficient order) — tying the timing back to the $n^3/3$-versus-$4n^3/3$ comparison
from Problem 1, and asking how many digits of $\hat\beta$ the two routes agree on.

**Two-stage least squares** (Fall 2024, Problem 3). Instrumental-variables regression is written as
$$\hat{X} = Z(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}X, \qquad \hat{\beta} = (\hat{X}^{\top}\hat{X})^{-1}\hat{X}^{\top}Y,$$
projecting $X$ onto the instrument $Z$ before regressing $Y$ on the projection. The problem sets
$Z$ at 60 million by 630 and $X$ at 60 million by 600, both sparse. Computing $\hat X$ as written
would form an explicit $60{,}000{,}000\times 600$ matrix — and, as the problem's own note points
out, the product of two sparse matrices need not be sparse, so even an intermediate matrix in a
literal two-stage computation can be dense at a scale that will not fit in memory. The exercise is
to say why the naive two-step computation fails at this scale and to rewrite the two equations into
a form that can actually be evaluated with sparse-matrix operations.

**Constrained least squares / quadratic programming** (Fall 2025, Problem 3). Minimizing
$(Y-X\beta)^{\top}(Y-X\beta)$ subject to $m$ linear equality constraints $A\beta=b$ (an $m\times p$
matrix $A$, $X$ of size $n\times p$) is a quadratic program, and the problem supplies the solution a
Lagrange-multiplier derivation produces:
$$\hat{\beta}=C^{-1}d+C^{-1}A^{\top}(AC^{-1}A^{\top})^{-1}(-AC^{-1}d+b), \qquad C=X^{\top}X,\ d=X^{\top}Y.$$
As written this needs $C^{-1}$ applied to two different vectors and once more inside another
inverse — three occasions to reuse a single factorization of $C$ rather than inverting it. The
exercise is to lay out, in pseudo-code and then in a Python function, which quantities can share one
factorization and which order of operations avoids recomputing anything.

All three problems have the same shape: a formula with an inverse in it, a factorization that
computes what the inverse is really being used for, and the discipline of solving a system once and
reusing the factorization rather than forming $M^{-1}$ and treating it as an ordinary matrix.

## Condition numbers: how many digits the two routes actually agree on

Every timing comparison in both problem sets is paired with a numerical-agreement question, and
both years use the same definition, stated directly in Fall 2024's Problem 4: the condition number
for solving $Ax=b$ is the ratio of the largest to the smallest magnitude eigenvalues of $A$. The
recurring ask — compare $\hat\beta$ from GLS via factorizations against $\hat\beta$ via the direct
inverse (Fall 2024, Problem 2c), or compare $x$ from `np.linalg.solve` against $x$ from Cholesky
(Fall 2025, Problem 2c) — is to count how many digits of the two answers actually agree and connect
that number to the condition number of the matrix involved, rather than assume that two
mathematically equivalent formulas give numerically identical answers on a computer.

Fall 2024's extra-credit problem (Problem 4) asks for the fact that makes the condition number
computable in the first place: that the induced $L_2$ matrix norm,
$$\|A\|_{2}=\sup_{z:\|z\|_{2}=1}\sqrt{(Az)^{\top}Az},$$
equals the largest absolute eigenvalue of $A$ when $A$ is symmetric. It is left as an exercise with
hints, not solved here.

## Fall 2024 and Fall 2025 side by side

| | Fall 2024 | Fall 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Decomposition compared | $LU$ (via `dgesv`) vs. explicit inverse | `solve`/$LU$ vs. explicit inverse vs. Cholesky |
| Estimator using the idea | generalized least squares | plain $x=A^{-1}b$, then constrained least squares |
| Sparse-matrix problem | two-stage least squares at $n=60$ million | none |
| Condition-number question | GLS: factorized vs. inverted $\hat\beta$ | `solve` vs. Cholesky $x$ |
| Extra credit | prove $\|A\|_2=$ largest $|\lambda|$ for symmetric $A$ | none |
| Parallel BLAS timing | not asked | timing vs. number of cores (Problem 2b) |

The Fall 2025 set adds a question the 2024 set does not ask: how the three methods' timings scale
with the number of threads available to a parallelized BLAS, pointing to Unit 10 §6.1 and Unit 6 §5
for getting a parallel BLAS running on the department's compute cluster (the SCF).

## Exercises

Rewritten cleanly from each year's problem set; not solved here.

### Fall 2024

1. Solving $Ax=b$ by Gaussian elimination (the $LU$ decomposition) costs $n^3/3$ operations (plus
   lower-order terms). Suppose instead you explicitly invert $A$ and then multiply: `numpy.linalg`'s
   `inv` does this by solving $AZ=I$ for $Z=A^{-1}$ using LAPACK's `dgesv`, which itself uses the
   $LU$ decomposition. Count the operations for (a) reducing $AZ=I$ to $UZ=I^*$ (where $I^*$ is no
   longer diagonal), (b) solving for $Z$ given $UZ=I^*$, and (c) computing $x=Zb$. Add these up and
   compare the total to the $n^3/3$ cost of solving $Ax=b$ directly.

   You may combine results already derived in class about Gaussian elimination and backsolves
   without re-deriving them. You do not need to exploit the fact that $I$ is diagonal — treat the
   right-hand side as an arbitrary matrix, as `dgesv` does. (Exploiting that structure would save a
   further $n^3/3$ operations.)

2. The generalized least squares estimator is
   $$\hat{\beta}=(X^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}Y,$$
   with $X$ an $n\times p$ matrix, $\Sigma$ an $n\times n$ positive-definite matrix, $n$ possibly in
   the thousands and $p$ in the hundreds.

   a. Write pseudo-code for an efficient computation of $\hat\beta$ — the specific linear-algebra
      steps and their order — then implement it as a Python function `gls()`, using high-level
      matrix-decomposition and linear-system-solving routines but no existing GLS implementation.
      (numpy's and scipy's Cholesky routines do not return the factor in the same form.)

   b. Compare your approach against computing $\hat\beta$ directly with the matrix inverse
      (computed only once, multiplied in an efficient order). Is the timing consistent with
      Problem 1 and with the efficiency results from Unit 10? Construct a positive-definite
      $\Sigma=W^{\top}W$ from a randomly generated $n\times n$ matrix $W$, and generate $X$ and $Y$
      randomly.

   c. Do the two approaches give the same $\hat\beta$ numerically, up to machine precision? Comment
      on how many digits agree, and relate this to the condition number of the calculation.

3. Two-stage least squares (2SLS) implements the instrumental-variables method used in economics:
   $$\hat{X} = Z(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}X, \qquad \hat{\beta} = (\hat{X}^{\top}\hat{X})^{-1}\hat{X}^{\top}Y,$$
   i.e., regress $Y$ on $X$ after keeping only the variation in $X$ correlated with instrument $Z$.
   An economics graduate student has $Z$ (60 million $\times$ 630), $X$ (60 million $\times$ 600),
   and $Y$ (60 million $\times$ 1), where $Z$ and $X$ are both sparse.

   a. Explain briefly why this cannot be computed in the two literal steps above, even using the
      efficient OLS techniques discussed in class for each stage.

   b. Rewrite the equations so that $\hat\beta$ can actually be computed without excessive memory
      use, assuming sparse-matrix multiplications can be done on the computer (e.g., via
      `scipy.sparse`). Describe the steps and/or give pseudo-code. (The product of two sparse
      matrices need not itself be sparse — and would not be, here.)

4. *(Extra credit.)* The condition number for solving $Ax=b$ is the ratio of the largest to the
   smallest magnitude eigenvalues of $A$. Show that the induced $L_2$ matrix norm,
   $$\|A\|_{2}=\sup_{z:\|z\|_{2}=1}\sqrt{(Az)^{\top}Az},$$
   equals the largest absolute eigenvalue of $A$ when $A$ is symmetric. (Treat "sup" as "max" if
   unfamiliar with the former — it handles cases like the supremum of the open interval $(0,1)$,
   which is $1$ even though no maximum exists.) Hint: writing $\Gamma$ for the orthogonal matrix
   diagonalizing $A$, set $y=\Gamma^{\top}z$ and show $\|z\|_2=1 \Rightarrow \|y\|_2=1$; then, given
   $y^{\top}Dy$ for diagonal $D$, think about how to maximize it subject to $\|y\|_2=1$.

### Fall 2025

1. Work out the exact operation count (multiplications plus divisions, including the constant, not
   just the order — e.g. $5n^3/2+8n^2$, not $O(n^3)$) for the Cholesky decomposition presented in
   Unit 10. Ignore square roots, additions and subtractions, and pivoting, and do not count any
   step that multiplies by $0$ or $1$. Compare your result to the count given in the notes.

2. Compare the speed of computing $x=A^{-1}b$ three ways: (i) `np.linalg.inv(A) @ b`,
   (ii) `np.linalg.solve(A, b)`, and (iii) a Cholesky decomposition followed by solving the two
   resulting triangular systems. Construct a positive-definite test matrix as $A=W^{\top}W$ for a
   randomly generated $n\times n$ matrix $W$.

   a. Using a single thread and $n=5000$, how do the timings and their relative ordering compare
      to the operation counts discussed in class and in the notes? (The full matrix inversion via
      the $LU$ decomposition costs $4n^3/3$.)

   b. How does the timing of each of the three approaches scale with the number of cores (threads)
      available to a parallelized BLAS? You may need the department's SCF cluster to guarantee a
      parallel BLAS — see Unit 10 §6.1 and/or Unit 6 §5.

   c. Do methods (ii) and (iii) give the same $x$ numerically, up to machine precision? Comment on
      how many digits agree, and relate this to the condition number of the calculation. Use a
      smaller $n$ than 5000 if needed to make estimating the condition number fast enough.

3. Least squares regression with an equality-constrained coefficient vector — minimizing
   $(Y-X\beta)^{\top}(Y-X\beta)$ subject to $A\beta=b$ for an $m\times p$ constraint matrix $A$
   ($X$ is $n\times p$) — is a form of quadratic programming. A Lagrange-multiplier derivation
   (covered later, in Unit 11) gives
   $$\hat{\beta}=C^{-1}d+C^{-1}A^{\top}(AC^{-1}A^{\top})^{-1}(-AC^{-1}d+b), \qquad C=X^{\top}X,\ d=X^{\top}Y.$$

   a. Describe, in pseudo-code, how you would implement this efficiently, applying the principles
      about matrix inverses and factorizations discussed in class.

   b. Write a Python function computing $\hat\beta$ efficiently using numpy's or scipy's matrix
      decomposition/manipulation routines. (In practice, an efficient solution matters most when
      the number of regression coefficients $p$ is large.)
